inline.s: Ninth month. On the first day, the same as before; also the birthday of the Southern Dipper. On the third, the birthday of the God of Pestilence; also the Dipper's descent. On the ninth, the birthday of Doumu; and again from the first to the ninth, the birthday of the Nine Emperors — whoever transgresses has his reckoning shortened. On the fifteenth, the same as before. On the seventeenth, the birthday of the Four Great Kings, the Golden Dragons. On the twenty-seventh, the Dipper's descent. On the twenty-eighth, the same as before. On the thirtieth, the same as before; also the birthday of the Medicine Buddha.

Tenth month. On the first day, the People's Year-End La. On the third, the Dipper's descent. On the fifth, the Lower Assembly; also the birthday of Bodhidharma. On the tenth, the descent of the Western Heaven King — whoever transgresses dies within a year. On the fifteenth, the birthday of the Water Official of the Lower Prime — whoever transgresses has his reckoning shortened. On the twenty-seventh, the birthday of the Great Emperor Ziwei of the North Pole; also the Dipper's descent. On the twenty-eighth, the same as before. On the thirtieth, the same as before.

Eleventh month. On the first day, the same as before. On the third, the Dipper's descent. On the sixth, the birthday of the Great Emperor of the Western Peak. On the eleventh, the birthday of the Great Heavenly Worthy Taiyi Who Saves from Suffering. On the fifteenth, the same as before. On the seventeenth, the birthday of Amitābha Buddha — whoever transgresses has his reckoning shortened. On the nineteenth, the birthday of the Great Heavenly Worthy of the Sun Palace. On the twenty-fifth, the descent of the Recording and Expelling Officer — whoever transgresses meets with calamity. On the twenty-seventh, the Dipper's descent. On the twenty-eighth, the same as before. On the thirtieth, the same as before.

Twelfth month. On the first day, the Prince's La. On the third, the Dipper's descent. On the fifteenth, the same as before. On the sixteenth, the birthday of the Great Emperor of the Southern Peak. On the twenty-first, the birthday of the Heavenly Worthy Tianyou. On the twenty-fourth, the Stove Lord of Destiny ascends to Heaven. On the twenty-fifth, the Three Pure Ones and the Jade Emperor descend together. On the twenty-seventh, the Dipper's descent. On the twenty-eighth, the same as before. On the thirtieth, all the gods descend to inspect good and evil — whoever transgresses has his reckoning shortened.

The birthdays of the holy and divine are exceedingly many; here I record only the chief among them. If one can observe them all, one may attain a great span of years. If one cannot observe them all, then for those noted as shortening the reckoning, transgression will surely cut short one's years. Further: the four beginnings of the seasons, the two equinoxes, the two solstices, the days of the earth-god sacrifices, the three fu days, the jiazi and gengshen days, the bingzi and bingding days, the days of the half-moons, the birthdays and death-days of one's ancestors and parents, one's own birthday, the days of one's own and one's ancestors' and parents' natal stars, days of great wind and great rain, great cold and great heat, thunder and lightning, days when heaven and earth are dark and dim, eclipses of the sun and moon, days of rainbow and earthquake, and the places of the mountain and river gods, the earth-god altars, the wells and the stoves, and whoever lets the lamp go out — also human affairs: drunkenness and surfeit, joy, anger, sorrow, dread, grief and fear, before birth and after birth, and the coming of the menses. All these belong to the taboos of Heaven, the taboos of Earth, and the taboos of Man. Whoever transgresses one of them: in great matters, his emolument is cut and his years reduced, or the children he begets do not live, or are born with bodies incomplete; in small matters, illness, hardship, and misfortune, injury to the body and suffering. Take heed. Take heed.

A poisonous heart already makes a man unbearable; a kindly face makes him unfathomable besides. No man but avoids the tiger and wolf, and all dread the snake and scorpion, for their venom. But when the heart is poison and the face is kind, warm and affectionate toward others, making himself pleasant to approach, and then lets loose his venom when no defense is possible — such treacherous venom is worse than that of tigers, wolves, snakes, and scorpions. At death he falls into the three evil paths swift as an arrow; life after life he draws retribution, suffering without end. How can one not take warning?

Cai Yuandu wore a face of spring breeze before his guests; even those he hated he treated with unbroken warmth and closeness, so that none could fathom him, and men called him the Smiling Yaksha. Later he died in demotion and exile. Such men are to be found everywhere. One should keep oneself within righteousness, treat them with courtesy, and steer them all with one even mind; then though they be venomous, how could their harm reach me?

Yu Tieqiao said: When a man's eyes look downward and he utters not a word, and between his brows there is no trace of the calm, still, compassionate air of a man of the Way, he must be a man of poisonous heart. Those who choose their friends should keep far from him and avoid him. Once there was a man who lay down at noon, and his spirit came out from his nostrils and turned into a black viper that coiled and came and went; all saw it. When he died afterward, his whole body burst open and was covered in snake's skin — just such a man. If he could but know his own venom and bitterly scour it away, as a good physician treats a boil, drawing out all the poison and only then stopping, he might still enter the Way. But he will certainly refuse to do it. What is to be done about such a man? Truly he is to be pitied.

Foul food: perhaps it was carelessly prepared, or worms have crawled in it and rats have gnawed it, or it has stood overnight and into the next day until its color and taste have changed. Eating it is enough to cause disease and harm the body. If one feeds it to others, they will surely be angry, and the gods too will loathe it. As for the servants in a household who waste water and broth, cooking far more food than is needed, and throwing away what is foul until the latrine is full — this is a great sin indeed, and the guilt for it falls mostly upon the master of the house. How can one not warn one another?

In the market of Hangzhou a roast goose was coiled about by a poisonous snake. A certain schoolmaster saw it and thought that whoever ate it would surely take in the poison. He wished to buy it, and the price named was two hundred; he had only a hundred cash on him, so he borrowed the rest from a neighbor he knew, and went with him to bury it. When they opened the earth they found a great ingot of red gold. The neighbor said, “It was I who hid this.” The wine-shop keeper said, “It is what I lost.” Just then the county magistrate arrived, and having questioned and learned the whole matter, he sighed and said: “Plainly this is the working of a good thought. You who would wrangle to monopolize the profit are all of you defying Heaven.” He had each of them caned, and gave the gold to the schoolmaster.

A certain scholar of Huai'an was cunning and treacherous and fond of sport. He broke into a house and caught hairless young mice; he minced them and pickled them in wine lees to serve to his boon companions, saying, “This is a sea delicacy.” Things of this kind that he did were not a few. Later his enemies seized him, bound him to a tree, and made him eat the dung of men, beasts, birds, and fowl; when he would not, they beat him cruelly, and he tasted it all through before they let him be. The retribution of evildoing follows each after its own kind.

Li Ji, a clerk of Qianzhou, lent money at interest far and wide. He had a servant who was sent to demand a debt; unable to get the money, the servant bound the debtor to a tree and poured filth-water over him, and so obtained a thousand coins. Suddenly lightning struck this servant before the gate of the Pu'an Temple. The money was at his waist, and it drove into his flesh, with skin grown over it. This case warns not only those who defile others but also wicked servants. For when a domineering slave uses his master's power to demand debts, he will force his way even into a woman's chambers, strip the last vestige of dignity from a man, and often bring about a great calamity. How can the thunderbolt's axe be kept forever over their heads?

Yu Yubi said: The Way is the upright road that all men must walk together. The Way of the sages of the Three Teachings, though their traces differ, agrees as if spoken by one mouth: the highest of them makes men understand the mind and see the nature; the next makes men turn from evil to good. None of them loves to make strange and uncanny things to delude men. Those who come forth from what is not upright and delude the people are all heterodox paths. Such were Zhang Jiao of the Han; Sun En and Lu Xun of the Jin; the Red Turbans and Liu Futong at the end of the Yuan; and in recent times the Wuwei, Huangtian, White Lotus, and the like. Their hearts are set on what is not upright; they bewitch and confuse the foolish folk, defy the ruler and turn their backs on kin, breed disaster and plant evil. These are the deeds of rebellious ministers and traitorous sons; the law of the state will surely put them to the slaughter, and the retribution of the underworld is that they do not escape. As for shamans and sorcerers with depraved arts, who falsely invoke the gods, speak recklessly of calamity and fortune, and stir up and deceive the people, their guilt is of the same kind.

Song Zixian of the Sui dynasty was skilled in many illusions. He made a light shine from a tower and transformed himself into the form of a Buddha, claiming that Maitreya had come into the world. He also hung a mirror in his hall, and whoever came to visit him he had look into it; their future lives appeared as the forms of snakes and beasts. He taught them to bow in worship, and then the human form appeared. Thus he gathered several thousand men, put himself at their head, and raised rebellion. When the government troops came to seize him, the ground all around his dwelling was a pit of fire, so that no one dared go in. The commander said: “This place never had any pit; it is nothing but witchery.” When they advanced, there was indeed no fire, and they took him and cut him to pieces.

A Daoist of Mount Qingcheng had arts of illusion. He drew the sons of the rich and noble to follow him and roam in a secluded courtyard, where he burned incense and set up curtains and worked his spells; and then the Goddess of Mount Wu and all the immortal maidens came at his summons. They drank and feasted and lay down together, no different from living people; when the laughter and pleasure were done, they trod the clouds and departed. He had his disciples watch through a crack in the wall. The young lord of Shu seized him but could not catch him; only when they carried pig's and dog's blood with them did they overtake him. Thrown into prison and tortured, he confessed: “Year after year I have taken virgins from among the people and given free rein to the arts of sexual congress, and the dead are without number.” Thereupon he was torn apart.

Yan Maoyou of the Ming said: He who obtains a sorcerer's art by which he could deceive the world and does not transmit it gains merit beyond measure. The ancients said: He who obtains the art of invisibility and does not try it for three years will surely become an immortal. They said also: If a lord has the art of making gold and does not use it, he will surely enter the Way. For one who cultivates the truth takes the erasure of his traces and the hiding of his light, the saving of men and the rescue of the world, as his chief aim. If he leans on some petty trick to dazzle and bewilder others, then the root of fame and profit is not yet pulled out, and he is far from the Way — how much more so one who does evil and practices imposture! In the bright light of day, how could such goblins be allowed to show their forms?

The Buddhist Three Refuges are: I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, I take refuge in the Sangha. The most essential of these is the Dharma in the middle. While the Buddha was in the world, it was by this Dharma that he taught and delivered living beings; after the Buddha's entry into nirvāṇa, it is this Dharma that he left behind to deliver living beings. The Buddha proclaimed the Dharma, the Sangha transmits the Dharma. If one does not take refuge in the Sangha, from whom shall one hear the Dharma? And if one does not obtain the Dharma, by what shall one cultivate? Now, he who cultivates by the Buddha-Dharma himself and teaches others by the Buddha-Dharma, taking the ending of birth-and-death and the realization of bodhi as his aim — he is of the Sangha. But he who does not cultivate by the Buddha-Dharma himself, who traffics in the Tathāgata to seek profit, fame, and offerings, and so misleads others — though he wears the square robe and shaves his crown and looks for all the world like a monk, he is in truth a son and grandson of Māra. A human body is hard to obtain, the Buddha-Dharma hard to encounter. Since one has obtained a human body, one must surely take refuge in the Buddha. In ancient times men sought the Dharma from the Sangha; today one must first test the Sangha by the Dharma. Once one has found the Sangha, then with a mind that has died to all else one receives the teaching and cultivates. Where is the Dharma? The Dharma is in the scriptures. I beg you to begin with Master Lianchi and the Yunqi Dharma Collection.

These four lines all concern the petty man's pursuit of profit. The foot-rule, the bushel, and the steelyard exist to level prices and make human dealings fair. Yet some in the world keep two sets, taking in by the large and giving out by the small, taking in by the heavy and giving out by the light. Their whole heart is set on nothing but getting the better of the bargain. Who knows that in gaining half a fraction of advantage one loses a fraction of one's merit and virtue? And to profit myself by harming others must bring down the fire of Heaven's thunder — it is not for nothing. Or the master of the house may know nothing of it, while the sons and servants who handle the comings and goings secretly do it; but the guilt in the end returns to the master of the house. This one must not fail to examine.

Lord Fei Rongmin of the Yuan was frugal and upright, took delight in goodness, and loved to give. In his household the measures for weighing and measuring were of one single standard, and he had it engraved upon all his vessels: “Out by this, in by this — may sons and grandsons forever do the same.” Thereafter his descendants reverently kept the family rule, and generation after generation they were noble and eminent.

In Guangling there was an old woman named Wang who sold cloth and silk by a short measure. After she died, she appeared to her son in a dream and said: “All my life I cheated men with a short measure. The courts of the underworld have punished me by making me a cow in the house of the Hao family at Xixi. On my belly is the character Wang.” Her son searched until he came to the Hao house, and a cow had indeed been born there, with white hair on its belly forming the character Wang. The son redeemed it and brought it home. He offered it fine food and it would not eat; offered it fodder and it ate. Under a heavy load in the field it was at peace; kept idle it kicked and butted at everything and could not be still. Do those who seek profit with a darkened heart know of this karmic retribution?

In the Wanli era of the Ming, there was in Yangzhou a great shop for southern goods. Its master, at the point of death, charged his son, saying: “All my life I built this house upon one steelyard. That steelyard was made of ebony fitted together, hollow within and hidden full of mercury. When I sold, I tipped the mercury to the head of the beam; when I bought, I tipped it to the tail. Weighing in heavily and giving out lightly — that is how I came to wealth.” The son's heart was troubled, but he did not dare speak. When his father died, he at once burned the steelyard, and in the smoke a dragon took shape and rose to Heaven. Before long both of the son's two sons died, and he complained, saying: “My father's heart was unfair, yet he met with peace; now I am fair in giving and taking and dare not cheat, and I lose two sons instead. Is this the way of Heaven?” Suddenly he seemed to come to a government hall, where the presiding officer instructed him, saying: “Your father in his daily life gave out lightly and took in heavily, cheating men to fatten himself. What he gained was lavish, yet it was also what was his by right; but because he made karma with a cheating heart and offended Heaven, the High Emperor sent two stars, Waste and Scatter, to be your sons: grown up, they would spend your fortune, and fire would follow, until your wealth was ended and your line cut off, to show forth the retribution. Now that you can mend your evil and cover your fault, and in all things are fair and kindly, the High Emperor has therefore taken back those two stars, and before long will give you in exchange two good sons to glorify your house. You must strive hard at doing good, and not complain or bear grudges rashly.” He woke and recorded it all, and gave himself the more to good works. Within three years he had two sons, both of whom passed the imperial examination, and his descendants were many and flourishing. Zhang Gongchen said: “I was at the Hanguan pass and was on friendly terms with this gentleman's descendants, and so I know the matter in great detail; the names are omitted to spare the feelings of kinsmen and friends about past faults.”

Xie Xiulin of Yulin used short measures and light steelyards, giving out lightly and taking in by force. One day he was struck dead by lightning. Time and again he was buried and time and again the grave burst open; when the flesh had rotted away they burned him, and in his belly they found a thunderbolt wedge.

Wang Liangru of the Song died and came back to life. He said that he had gone to the courts of darkness and seen bushels, measures, steelyards, and rules hung upon the wall. He asked what they were for. The clerk of the underworld said: “For the high and the low, the light and the heavy — those who cheat in their hearts and scheme for profit receive their guilt here.” Ten days after Liangru was restored to life, all the bushels, steelyards, and the like used by the brokers that were not of the lawful standard were destroyed by fire.

Li Jue of Guangling in the Song made his living by trade. When he saw others of the same calling giving out lightly and taking in heavily, letting out by the small and taking in by the large, his heart loathed it, and he admonished them and stopped them. Jue himself gave and took alike, taking only a thin profit to support his mouth and belly. As the years deepened, his house too grew rich. Later a commissioner of the Jiang-Huai region whose name and surname were the same dreamed one night that he entered a cave-dwelling and saw in the register of immortals the name Li Jue. He was overjoyed, thinking that one day he would mount to immortality. Suddenly two boy attendants said: “This Li Jue is not Your Excellency; he is a commoner of Guangling.” Waking, he sought out the man, and asked what he cultivated. He said: “Nothing else — I only keep my heart level in dealing with things.” Later he lived to the age of a hundred and, casting off his corpse, became an immortal. Zhu Zhen said: “The world says, do not cheat the gods. I say it is not the hundred gods of Heaven and Earth — only do not cheat the god within your own heart; that is not cheating the gods.” Alas, how many are there who can understand this?

Li Yongzheng of Shu was skilled at making bushels and steelyards, light or heavy, increased or diminished, exactly as men ordered; he took double their price, and there was nothing he would not do. Petty men with no regard for the way of Heaven came to him again and again. The divine inspector of affairs impeached him, and Yongzheng and his two sons all went blind; the five fingers of each were maimed and crippled, and the joints of their hands fell away and they died. Alas! Such is the retribution for one who makes such things for others. This is the way of punishing the root. Of all who make a living, who does not wish to nourish his body and his household? Yet why do they go again and again to offend Heaven's anger? How good it would be if all could take warning from this case and fiercely reform.

In the markets of late, of the goods traded, the false almost outnumber the true. This too is a change in the way of the world and the heart of man. In all that is needed for food and drink, in the use of medicines, in gold and silk and vessels of every kind, the slightest deceit and error means the loss of one's heart and harm to others, and nothing is worse than this. As for passing false silver, its evil is still greater, and Heaven's punishment swifter.

In the gengxu year of the Kangxi era of the Qing, a man of Fujian surnamed Gu, lodging in Jiangyin, secretly sold counterfeit silver. He carried it to market, and no one could tell it; only it could not last past ten days, after which it showed its true substance again. A certain man exchanged six pieces of silver for twenty and went to Changmen to buy gauze and satin. On the boat home, as he passed Huadang by night, the wind rose and the boat capsized, and not an inch of silk survived. The man was lucky to be a good swimmer and escaped with his life, returning home naked. Gu too on that same day was struck dead by lightning, and the furnace and hammers for making the silver were shattered to powder. Alas, how foolish! That Gu was punished for his wicked art is only what he deserved. But the other, by a single thought of greed, in a moment lost the six pieces of silver he had, and of his clothes, bedding, and baggage one cannot even guess how many pieces of silver they were worth. Business come to this may be called a losing venture indeed; and that he did not lose his life in the waves was a narrow thing. Senseless petty men are pitiable in this way. I have one saying to wake men up: “I trade because I wish to live. I wish to live — do others not wish to live? I wish to nourish my family and keep its mouths fed — do others alone not wish to nourish their families and keep their mouths fed? And moreover, for the man who cheats his heart and defies Heaven, retribution is bright and plain: there is none who does not die and bring ruin and extinction upon his household.” Is this not far from the true heart of a trader?

The grandfather of Sun Shenchuan, Minister of the Six Boards, one day in the course of trade took in two taels of silver. The old gentleman held it up to show to others — it was counterfeit silver. He thought: since this silver cannot be used, how can I keep it to deceive others? He went to the bank of the Eastern River, and there walked several tens of paces into the water and cast it into the deep. His son passed the imperial examination and became a vice commissioner. That Sun was Shenchuan himself. Old Master Sun got the silver and threw it into the lake; his heart was one with that of Patriarch Lü. That his sons and grandsons were eminent and noble is still the lesser part of the reward.

Lu Chang of Mount Lu in the Song sold oil and candles, mixing fish fat into them; Huang Yu of the Jianlong Abbey put beef tallow into the oil to make candles. Both men were struck dead by Heaven's thunder. Alas! Those today who mix sand into the salt they sell, or water into the wine they sell, and the like — let them take warning from this at the side.

A certain man of Haiyan named Ni ground up scraps of common wood and made incense to sell. One night the incense powder suddenly burst into smoke and flame. Ni wished to get out of the door, but the smoke bewildered him so that he could not, and the man and the house were both burned to ashes.

Zhang Anguo of the Ming, when he was magistrate of Fuzhou, because many in the markets sold counterfeit medicines, issued a proclamation warning them, saying: “Tao Hongjing and Master Sun, by the Materia Medica and the Thousand Ducat Formulas, saved living things and benefited the living and laid up much hidden merit, and their names stand among the immortals. From that time to this, those who practice medicine and sell drugs and sincerely rescue men have obtained blessing and reward in great numbers. Not to speak of what the books record — take only recent times: the proof is even more plentiful. There are those who sold nothing but true medicine and at once had wealth of tens of thousands, or themselves lived in peace and honor and enjoyed a great age, or whose sons and grandsons passed the examinations and changed the standing of their house. It follows like shadow to form, with no error. And I have seen with my own eyes those who sold counterfeit medicines. At first they laid up a little property and thought themselves clever; they did not know that in the hidden dark their own allotted wealth and emolument were all being cut away; that they themselves met with many sudden calamities, or their sons and grandsons squandered and ruined all beyond reason, so that some met with the fire of Heaven and were struck by thunder. The reason is that those who buy medicine are mostly in the urgency of illness, and so they bring their money and beg for help; dutiful sons and obedient grandsons hope only that one dose will bring relief. Yet they are cheated and deluded by false medicine: not only is there no benefit, but harm comes instead. To kill a single bird or beast in ordinary times still has its cause and effect; how much more, among the ten thousand things, is human life the heaviest. To be brought to ruin without cause — how endless is the pain. How can one not take warning?”

To take by cunning speech; to profit by wickedness — then the cruelty and meanness of such a heart knows no limit. All those today who haunt the boat landings, who knock at the wooden bell, who traffic in gossip and in the passing of bribes, are of this kind. One need not point only to the private coining of money and the private boiling of salt before calling it the reaping of wicked profit. Therefore even among the capped and gowned there is this evil; how can one blame only the petty folk of the marketplace?

An ancient poem says:
The more cunning and clever, the poorer men grow;
Cunning and clever Heaven will not allow.
If wealth and honor came by cunning and guile,
Then the world's dull fellows would swallow the west wind.

Zhang Feng practiced the writing of legal documents and knew in detail the land taxes and household registers of the region. He could make a man whose fields stretched to the horizon empty his purse, and a household without a foot of ground suddenly fill the registers. The region suffered from his poison but dared not speak: speak in the morning, and by evening the tax assessment would come. He was especially skilled in the arts of fleecing the people. Whenever a chief magistrate arrived, he would at once summon him and question him; then he would take his hand in warm friendliness; in the end he commanded him with a nod, and the man obeyed. Day by day he taught the chief magistrate to squeeze out the people's wealth to the last drop. The magistrate took two parts of it, and seven went to Feng. The grand coordinator Lord Tang, learning the facts of the case, sent armed men to bind him. As he was being taken along the road he offered the guards a rich bribe, and they refused it; so he schemed to slip away, and the guards chased him but could not catch him. At that moment there was not a cloud in the four quarters, when with a crack of thunder it struck in the east, and Feng fell dead in the west. His belly was as if slit open and his five viscera as if scooped out. Men were too disgusted to gather up the body, and dogs and pigs left it where it lay.

Those who are servants and slaves today are men of former lives who made karma and piled up evil until it overflowed the measure of one thousand eight hundred. But if one who was truly never a servant or slave, being by origin a son or daughter of good family, is forced by my power and influence to become a servant or slave, then that is to press the good down into the base. As for selling the good into prostitution, that belongs among the ten unpardonable crimes, and need not even be spoken of.

Zhou Xiang of Zhangzhou was a friend of Xue Chun. Chun was poor, and had only one son. When Chun died, the son went to Xiang — and Xiang made him a slave. When the boy was the least bit disobedient, he laid on the whip cruelly. One day Xiang met Chun on the road and started back, saying: “Brother, you have already departed this world — why are you here among men?” Chun said: “I have come to see my son, and to urge you along as well.” Xiang's sweat poured down like rain. He went home and died suddenly. One often sees houses of wealth and honor where kinsmen in hardship and with no one to turn to lodge under their roof and depend on them for food and clothing, and who are made to do the work of servants, or even reviled and cursed besides. This too belongs to the kind of thing the Supreme One warns against. Yet such men begin with a heart of relief and pity and end by doing the work of destruction: not only do they win no merit, they also lose their virtue. Is this not to be lamented?

The Guangji Granary of Zhejiang province each year assigned the great households of Hangzhou to serve as granary clerks and manage its receipts and disbursements. One man embezzled so much of the government money that he had no way to repay it. The prefect's judge, a certain Wang, then seized his wife, concubines, sons, and daughters for the government; still the debt could not be repaid. So he had them carried in a small boat onto West Lake to serve as waiting-maids for the pleasure of visitors, and the money they earned was paid into the government. Later Wang's own sons and grandsons included those who became prostitutes.

There is one kind of parent who, driven to a deed that loses all heart and all shame, sells son or daughter in the hope that they will become servants. But can my own heart bear it? A man of good conscience who has the means to scatter gold should relieve their emergency and preserve their goodness — this is abundant virtue. And even if he cannot, let me not treat them with contempt; though they must be sold to another, still I shall not have failed to do all that is in my heart.

The good and the base were never fixed by nature. It is only that the sons and daughters of the poor are sold to the rich, and so they are called base. In truth they are all good. Yet men today cherish their own sons and daughters like pearls: fine grain and rich fare, gauze and brocade and embroidery. And toward their adopted sons and daughters and the like: clods of earth and the whip, coarse fare and hunger, rags and cold. They too were born of parents. Why are they not treated with the same fairness? Do they never think that the rich may become poor and the poor may become rich — the way of Heaven is not to be known in advance — and that one cannot be sure the good will not turn base, nor the base turn good?

In receiving men and in dealing with those below you, you must, when you stand in a place of wealth and honor, know fully the aches and stings of poverty and lowliness; in the time of your youth and strength, think on the bitterness of age and decline; dwelling in a place of ease and joy, feel for the circumstances of calamity and hardship; standing as a bystander, forgive the bitter heart of those caught within the game.

To deceive is to cheat men when they neither know nor see. To take by surprise is the look of one quick and nimble. Whoever uses treacherous schemes and sets snares so that men fall into his trap — that is called cheating and surprising. Neither cheating nor surprising may be used; and to use them upon a fool is the more pitiable. Though the fool cannot repay it, in the hidden dark there is one who repays it in his stead. In the fool there is no loss; but I have lost first.

The Yuan Family Precepts say: Poverty and wealth have no fixed course, and fields and houses no fixed owner. With money one buys, without money one sells. The household that buys property should understand this principle. And when a man sells his property, it may be for want of food, or because of debt, or for sickness and death, marriage and litigation; because he has expenses of a thousand, he sells property worth a thousand. The buyer should be generous and liberal, and pay him his price at once; then even though it passes out of his hands and he keeps nothing, it is still enough for him to settle that one matter. But the man who is rich and without benevolence makes it his whole business to cheat and surprise: knowing that the other needs the money urgently, he openly refuses while secretly luring him on, and strangles the price. When the contract is made, he delays and does not pay the whole at once; or he pays it off in grain or other goods at a high price; or he sets a term and pays it out in fragments. The household that sold the property scatters it again at once and cannot settle a single matter, and the going and coming to demand payment, and the cost of men and strength, take up half of it again. And the rich man secretly rejoices, thinking himself a fine schemer — not knowing that the way of Heaven loves to return, and that on some it is repaid in their own persons, and on some in their sons and grandsons. Men are mostly deluded and do not wake. Why is it so?

To take things in by the mouth is called greed: it means that a man's covetousness, like the mouth eating food, knows no satiety and no limit. Laozi said: No sin is greater than many desires; no calamity is greater than not knowing when one has enough. He who knows enough is happy even in poverty and lowliness; he who does not know enough is anxious even in wealth and honor. Men of the world covet and seek until their measure overflows, and in the end it all scatters — that need not even be said; and besides, they drag down a whole field of calamity and sin, the harder to be finished with.

Zhen Bin was a man of good conduct. He once took a bundle of ramie to a shop and pledged it for money. Later, when he redeemed the ramie and brought it home, he found five taels of gold inside it. Bin returned it. The shopkeeper offered him half, and Bin would not take it, saying: “In the fifth month I wear a fur coat and carry firewood on my back — would I be one to accept lost gold?”

In the time of Emperor Daizong of the Tang, the Secretariat Attendant Yuan Zai let his sons take bribes and traffic in office. In the capital and in the provinces alike, loyal and good men were thrust aside and the greedy and base promoted. His wealth, luxury, and music and song were beyond what even the palace could match. The emperor warned him, and he would not mend. At last the emperor was angry, took Yuan Zai and by edict granted him death; his wife and children were granted death as well, and his house was confiscated. There were five hundred taels of stalactite, which by edict were divided among the officials of the Secretariat, the Chancellery, and the Censorate; and pepper to the amount of eight hundred bushels, with other things in like measure. Zheng Xuan said: “From ancient times, how many who held the office of chancellor ever died of hunger and cold? Yet they die time and again of wealth and goods. It is laughable.”

In the Tianshun era of the Ming, Li Ming of Jiaxing obtained a precious pot. The rich man Cao Yuan offered twenty bushels of rice for it, and Li would not consent. He went then to Huai Yue, who offered double, and still he would not sell. He went again to Wu Ruhui, who offered a hundred bushels of rice, and the bargain was all but agreed. There was one Liu Zhu, who said to Ming: “I have a plan that will bring you a great haul. If you present it as tribute to the eunuch superintendent Zhang, and scheme for the salt certificates of the whole prefecture of Jiaxing, the profit should be a hundredfold.” Ming agreed. Zhu worked the connections for him, and he did indeed obtain what he sought. The profit reckoned at more than three thousand taels, and Liu took a third of it. As Ming was carrying it home, his boat capsized crossing the river, and the certificates were all ruined and soaked. The prefect of Jiaxing, Yang Jizong, pressed for the recovery of the former certificates, and Ming died in prison. Liu ruined his own property to repay it.

The ancients said: No man in the world lives a hundred years, yet in vain he makes plans for a thousand. What is the meaning of insatiable seeking? He means to plan for sons and grandsons. But he does not know the saying: If sons and grandsons are not my equals, what do they want money for? If sons and grandsons surpass me, what do they want money for?

Shu Guang of the Han said: “Do you think I am old and muddled and do not think of my sons and grandsons? I have old fields and a cottage; if my sons and grandsons till them diligently, they are enough to furnish food and clothing. If I add to them and make them a surplus, that is to teach my sons to be idle. When the worthy have much wealth, it injures their resolve; when the foolish have much wealth, it increases their faults. And the rich man is the resentment of the many. Since I have no way to teach my sons and grandsons, I do not wish to increase their faults and breed resentment.” From this we see it: Sima Wengong's teaching that laying up gold is not so good as laying up virtue — how can we fail to recite it well and put it into practice?

To curse is to swear before the gods; to seek vindication is to ask the gods for swift retribution. This need not take shape in a written petition; whoever in anger and contention rashly calls upon the gods is doing it. It is recorded in the Chapter on Oaths and Curses: whenever there is cursing, then from the four directions and the eight quarters a man is cursed, and all the fierce and evil ghosts get their chance and find their opening to work their harm. Unless one repents and begs the gods of Heaven to dissolve it, it is not easily cut off. If so, can cursing be done?

At the beginning of the Wanli era of the Ming, Wang Zhu, a village conscript of Xihua, quarreled with a taxpayer over arrears and swore an oath in the City God's temple. At night he lodged in the Yangshan Monastery. Suddenly he heard the shouts of an escort, and rising to look, he saw an official standing beneath a torch, in a black head-wrap and crimson robe, with a great throng of guards. The official called two strong men, who took up knives and came at Zhu. Zhu seized the inkstone from the table and hurled it at them, but he was pierced through nonetheless, and blood flowed from his mouth and cheeks. The monks of the monastery started up in alarm and saw no one. Then he knew it was the City God. The next morning he put on the garb of a prisoner and went to beg pardon. Looking at the images in the temple, they were exactly as in his dream, and the attendant on the right was the one who had held the knife, with the mark of ink still on him. A month later the sore in his mouth healed, but the scar of the knife remained plain. Now in any matter there is right and wrong; if one is in the right, then public judgment cannot be erased, and in time it becomes clear — what need to contend? And if one is in the wrong, then on self-examination one's heart is not at ease — how dare one face the gods and rail at others? Besides, in all matters one should only follow principle and rest in one's lot. Once one curses, the ghosts and gods loathe it, and Heaven's censure is sure to come. How can one not take warning?

Wine can disorder the nature; to be deeply addicted to it brings the greatest loss. Reading the Announcement on Wine, one knows how far the ancients looked in their care; reading the Odes on Wine, one knows how deep the ancients' lodging of their feelings. Even as the Ritual speaks of the offering of a single cup, host and guest bowing to each other, it is to guard against the failings of wine. Men of the world love wine without measure, until their bodies and frames are toppled, ritual and law thrown into disorder, cursing at the table and lying in the streets, defying law and offending superiors. In time they lose their hearts and their virtue. It can make a scholar ruin his name, an official lose his post, a farmer let his fields go wild, a merchant lose his capital, and in the worst case lose life and destroy the household. Is it not grievous? Fan Zhi, Duke Lu of the Song, warned his son, saying: “Take heed, do not be given to drink; the maddening drug is no goodly flavor. It can turn a careful and honest nature into a fierce and stubborn kind.” Cao Yuechuan said: “To nourish the nature, do not crave the water that clouds the nature; to build a household, beware the soup that breaks the household.” And the root of all lewdness and disorder springs mostly from wine; therefore among the four warnings wine is put first.

In the drunk all good thoughts are gone and evil thoughts blaze up. What in sobriety he would never dare do, never dare say, in drink he does and says at will. Therefore he who can drink in measure — his wine is called the broth of great harmony, the friend that forgets feeling. He who cannot drink in measure — his wine is called the soft demon, the sweet poison.

Wine is the firewood of lust. To give free rein to wine and not to lust is rare indeed. When the inner fire is blazing and the desire of lust flares up, it is hard enough to guard against; how much more when one indulges in wine to feed that fire? To take a woman when drunk and full — the five viscera are overturned and the sickness is no small matter. This above all should be sternly punished. And there are those who, drunk, give rein to lust and so meet with insult and lose their lives; repentance then comes too late.

Nothing in the world is more laughable than contending for victory and defeat over the wine table. In dealing with the world, in every matter one should yield; how much more in a casual gathering for pleasure, where passing the drinking order and matching fists is no more than a moment's excitement. To win is no glory; to lose is no disgrace; to be beaten is no loss; to beat is no gain. It is exactly as the chess players say: victory is gladness indeed, but defeat may also be a joy. Yet these men are dull and know it not, and will not stop until they have won — until they are not drunk they will not cease. How extreme is their folly! And there are those who boast of their capacity and make it a grand deed that no one can match them, not knowing that in their own virtue, learning, and literary work, and in rank and fame, there is much in which they do not match others; yet they boast only of capacity. Is this not absurd? There is yet another kind, who take pride in the strictness of their drinking rules. They never think that wine is for making merry and should be taken according to each man's measure; why force others to drink much and so injure their lives? The saying goes: Tyrannical government is fiercer than a tiger. I say a tyrannical drinking rule is the same. If there be such a man at the table, one should hurry to withdraw from him.

In the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom the failings of drinking are listed. They are: the mind knows no measure, one; wealth and goods are emptied out, two; the gate of many diseases, three; the root of strife, four; to go naked and barefoot, like cattle and horses, five; to dance wildly and curse at the table, hated and loathed by others, six; to fail to get what one ought to get, seven; to lose what one has got, eight; to tell out all one's secrets and repent when sober, nine; to make many mistakes in drink and feel shame when sober, ten; the body weak and strength soft, eleven; the complexion changing, twelve; the mind and will confused, thirteen; wisdom clouded, fourteen; not knowing to respect father and mother, fifteen; not knowing to respect the ghosts and gods, sixteen; not knowing to fear men's talk, seventeen; not knowing to fear the king's law, eighteen; factions and drunken violence, nineteen; estrangement from the worthy and good, twenty; no shame, twenty-one; quickness to rage, twenty-two; not keeping the six senses in check, twenty-three; giving free rein to lust without measure, twenty-four; being cast off by honorable men, twenty-five; having no careful caution or avoidance, twenty-six; making day into night so that all one's work is ruined, twenty-seven; committing offenses against the teachings of propriety, twenty-eight; casting away the good Dharma, twenty-nine; turning far from nirvāṇa, thirty; planting the cause of idiocy and madness, thirty-one; and at the breaking up of the body, at the end of life, falling into the evil paths, thirty-two. If one is again born a man, the mind is ever wild and disordered, and all outer goods and the means of living are utterly ruined.

A certain scholar Liu of Fujian was of strict and upright conduct and had very many pupils. In ordinary days he would always teach them to guard against lust. One day, having drunk by chance, he contended with a friend over a courtesan, and when he woke he repented greatly and was ashamed to face his students. He shut his door for three days and gathered all the cases, ancient and modern, of men ruined by wine, to warn himself, and called it the Classic of a Hundred Regrets. And a certain scholar Ye of Wu was by nature filial and friendly. One day after drinking he quarreled and cursed at his younger brother, and when his father came out to reason with him, he even spat out a word or two of insolence. When he woke at the fifth watch, his wife told him how he had been in his drunkenness, and his remorse and hatred were beyond bearing. He hurried to his father's room, knocked his head on the ground, wept and wailed, and knelt waiting to beg pardon, and only then did his father's anger dissolve. Ah! These two gentlemen were of mild and careful nature by habit, yet even they could not escape being perverse after drink; how much worse the case of the dissolute and depraved! Wine is well named the spring of calamity. Truly.

Wu Yu of the Song was commissioner of military affairs. At that time Chen Zhizhong was dismissed from the chancellorship and recommended Wu to take his place. At a banquet in attendance on the emperor, Wu fell asleep drunk; suddenly he stroked the couch and called for his attendants. The emperor was angry, and dismissed him to the Western Capital's retainers' office. Again Guo Zhi was assistant administrator; coming in for an audience, the smell of wine reeked over the imperial seat, and he was demoted to Nanjing.

To lose one's words after wine often brings great calamity. A certain notable of Wuxi County, young and of much talent, being drunk, exposed to a man's face the shameful secrets of his women's quarters. The man laughed easily and said: “It is only the talk of a drunkard.” He seemed not to mind in the least, and all at the table admired his forbearance. An experienced elder waited until the notable had gone, then said to those at the same table: “He who is angry is the ordinary man; he who smiles is not to be fathomed.” Half a year later the scholar was murdered by someone's plot, and all suspected that the man who held the knife was the one he had insulted before. Alas! Such are the calamities of wine. And as for falling into a river or a pit because of drink, splitting one's head or face, losing one's wealth, leaking secrets, offending the ghosts and gods — every kind of disaster and blame has wine for its cause. Why will men not give it up?

Su Yijian of the Song was a scholar of the Hanlin. Because he drank heavily he suffered a nosebleed and fell ill and died. And Wang Quan was a palace aide; from great drunkenness his navel split and he died. When the maddening drug soaks into a man, there are few who do not come down with illness; if it breaks out early the sickness is shallow, if it breaks out late the sickness is deep — but there is none it does not bring to death. Therefore, looking over all who have enjoyed a great span of years, none of them loved wine. Why will men deliver this body handed down by their forebears into a life of drunkenness and a death of dreams?

Chen Hao was fond of drink by nature and served as education commissioner of Shandong. His father sent him a letter warning him, and so he had a craftsman make a small cup and engraved words on it, saying: “By my father's command I give up wine; I shall drink only ten cups.”

The family rules of the Zheng clan of Pujiang: sons and grandsons under thirty years of age were not permitted to let wine touch their lips. Those in their prime might drink a little, but anyone who sank into drunkenness and clamor was sure to be caned. In serving guests, the only aim was sincerity and honesty; they did not force wine on them. The women of the house were not allowed to drink together; those past fifty might do as they pleased. This is fit to be a model for those who keep a household.

The ancients said: Wine means to approach. Approach what is right and one is right; approach what is wrong and one is wrong. Wine means to make. Make what is good and one is good; make what is evil and one is evil. So wine cannot of itself make a man right or wrong, good or evil; it is the man himself who makes himself right or wrong, good or evil. Can the two words “economy” and “measure” ever be dispensed with?

Zhang Gongyi of the Tang held nine generations under one roof, and it was all in a single word: forbearance. Quarreling comes of the lack of forbearance. Between flesh and blood, to insist on reason wounds the affection, and when the affection is wounded it is no longer reason. How can one quarrel rashly? Yet the source of it lies mostly in the words of women stirring up strife. For a woman's heart is not fair; she is ever nursing jealousy. And those she calls father-in-law and mother-in-law, elder and younger brothers-in-law, and sisters-in-law of her own generation, are all joined by circumstance and given their titles by force; they are not natural kindred by heaven. Therefore she makes light of cutting off affection and easily quarrels. The two sides pass each other's words back and forth until resentment piles up. Within one household discord and change spring up in clusters, and the matter has many branches that cannot be told in full. Only where the heavenly bonds are deep and true, and the man is of high and far-seeing understanding, illumining and penetrating all, will slander not be listened to; then naturally the harmonious air steams up and love and friendship are glad and full. What quarreling could there be?

Zheng Lian of Pujiang in the Ming kept a single household register for two hundred years without dividing, and men named his village the Village of Righteousness. The prefect set up a plaque over it reading: The First House Under Heaven. When Taizu came to the throne he summoned him to the capital and asked: “How many mouths does your household feed?” He answered: “A thousand and more.” The emperor said: “Truly the first house under Heaven.” At that time Empress Ma, hearing it from behind the screen, said to Taizu: “Your Majesty holds the empire, and it was one man who raised the matter. Now the Zheng family has a thousand and more in one house; would it not be easier for them to raise a matter?” The emperor was startled, and asked again: “Is there a way, sir, in your keeping the clan together?” Lian answered at once: “Nothing else — only that I do not listen to a wife's words.” The emperor could not help laughing aloud. At that time Henan presented fragrant pears, and the emperor gave him two. Lian lifted the pears in both hands above his head and hurried out. The emperor had him watched. When he reached home he called the clansmen together, faced the palace gate and knocked his head in thanks for the imperial grace, then set out two great vats of water, broke the pears into them, and gave them to all to drink. Taizu heard of it and was pleased. Later someone slandered the family for being in league with a powerful minister, and Taizu said: “The Zheng house is not like that; it is a false charge.” Later he had their sons and grandsons of thirty and above summoned to the capital and gave them all office. The clan head Ying came to the palace gate to thank him for the grace, and the emperor, at the Fengtian Gate, wrote with his own hand the three great characters “House of Filial Righteousness” and gave it to him, sealed with the imperial jade seal.

Loyalty means giving one's all to oneself; goodness is the name for uprightness. Of all things man is the most spiritual, and among men the male is held most noble. Since one has obtained this spiritual and noble body, to be treacherous and disloyal, perverse and not good, is not only to betray one's own spirit but to fail greatly toward the Creator.

Fan Zhongyan, Duke Wenzheng of the Song, lost his father at two years of age. When he was a little older he stood forth and made his own way, reciting and reading day and night, sitting still and thinking in silence, and in six years he mastered the Six Classics. At twenty he passed the imperial examination and became judge of Hezhong. His loyalty and love soaked into men's hearts. He served as vice minister and, in court and in the ordering of his household, used both kindness and authority. Loyal to his ruler and loving his country, his good deeds shine down. He taught his sons by the right way and relieved the poor and succored the suffering. His name shook his age and is revered for a hundred generations. The two words “a man” — truly he was not unworthy of them.

The Book of Rites says: The man leads, the woman follows. It says also: In youth she follows her father and elder brother; when married she follows her husband; when her husband dies she follows her son. The Family Instructions of Master Yan says: A woman's place is to preside over the kitchen and attend only to the rules of wine, food, and clothing. If she has intelligence and talent, she should only assist her husband and supply what he lacks. If she overrides her husband and meddles in affairs outside, she is the hen that crows at dawn, the owl with the long tongue, and the decline of the household begins there.

Yuan Kui of the Han married the eldest daughter of Ma Jichang, and the dowry sent with her was very rich. Kui said: “A wife's part is to hold the dustpan and broom — why need she be so overly precious and fine?” She answered: “My loving parents gave thought to it, and I did not dare defy their command. If you admire the high conduct of Bao Xuan and Liang Hong, I too will follow the righteousness of Shaojun and Meng Guang.”

Lady Hou, wife of Cheng Xiang of the Song, was modest and yielding, gentle and harmonious; even in small matters she would surely report and then act. She ordered her household by rule and did not beat the servants. If any of her sons reproved them, she would always warn him, saying: “High and low differ, but a human being is one and the same.” When Xiang was angry about something, she would always smooth it away for him. Only when her sons had faults would she not cover them, and she would often say: “A son's unworthiness comes of his mother hiding his fault, so that his father does not know of it.” Later her two sons, Yi and Hao, both became great Confucians, held high and noble office, and were offered sacrifice in the Temple of Confucius.

A certain resident of Hezhou kept more than a hundred geese. One day they ate his neighbor's rice, and the neighbor beat more than fifty of the geese to death. The man's wife saw it and was furious, but then she thought: “If I go to law with him, it will surely cost me money besides; and my husband is lying drunk, and if he learns of it and goes to beat the man, it will be even worse.” So she gathered up the dead geese and salted them. The next morning the neighbor suddenly died. When her husband learned of the day before, he was deeply moved and said: “If you had told me yesterday, I would have beaten him in my drunkenness — would that not have been a case of manslaughter?”

The Purple Mist Formula for Creating Blessing says: When a woman cultivates goodness it is no different from a man's; only, as a woman has no affairs outside the house, the three followings are her good. And if she has good deeds to do, it is best that she urge her parents and her husband to do them. Therefore, when father and mother have three good deeds, the daughter or wife takes a share of one; when the husband has two good deeds, the wife takes a share of one; and she who has thought of it beforehand shares the same merit. To urge and convert women to goodness is twice as hard and twice as meritorious as a woman doing good herself. When elder and younger sisters-in-law and sisters have good deeds, if they praise one another, their merit may be equal as well; what is precious is to rejoice with one heart and have no jealousy. If one can be filial and respectful, harmonious and yielding, assisting the husband and teaching the sons, and so fulfill one's own part, and then add to it deep faith in cause and effect, vegetarian eating, and Buddha-recitation, then in this present life body and mind will naturally be at peace and happy, sons and grandsons will flourish, and at the end of life one will surely receive the Buddha's compassionate guidance and be born in the West. One should only cultivate quietly at home and not go racing about outside: for one thing it does not waste one's time, for another it keeps one free of gossip. Again, when sons and grandsons are ill, to pray to the gods and offer sacrifice costs several pieces of silver at a stroke — how much better to do good in ordinary days and save living creatures, and so naturally obtain the gods' protection? Within the women's quarters there is a cave-heaven and a blessed land of its own. Make the effort and practice it.

When husband and wife are harmonious, the household prospers. A woman has never read books or understood principle; if she does wrong, one should clearly instruct her and make her understand. Certainly one must not let her have her own way without restraint, but neither should one at once conceive anger and loathing. Yet men of the world, meeting a fierce and violent wife, submit to her bullying; meeting a weak and simple wife, they tyrannize over her — fearing the strong and bullying the good. How can a true man do this? There are also foolish men who dote on a concubine and insult the wife, or cling to a courtesan and deceive the wife, and even beat and curse and rage at her. These above all will not come to a good end.

Yan Guangzhong said: In life let no one be born a woman's body, for every kind of sorrow and joy comes from others. She leaves her kin and parts from those she loves; in life and in death she follows another; the one she serves is her husband alone. Hungry, she does not eat alone; cold, she is not clothed alone. She gives up her own body to be mine, gives up her father and mother to be father and mother to mine. Should she light upon a merchant who travels far, or a scholar who goes abroad to study, then she keeps a lone room and sleeps alone, and on cold nights the bed is iron — is this easy to bear? And I, then, am fickle: I give my body to other houses, lodge my affection in the flowers and willows, and dote on them like a madman. Or perhaps one day I become noble and eminent, with concubines and maids before me in throngs; I give no thought to her who bound her hair with me; in fear I turn only to you, in joy I cast off the rest. Alas, why do we treat others without fellow-feeling? For the long-tongued wife who gives her will free rein and rides roughshod, and the woman of loose conduct who forgets all restraint and makes a scene, that is one thing. But when she serves her husband's parents, keeps peace with her sisters-in-law, is harmonious with her husband's aunts, and among those before and after her, wife and concubine alike, each has her own heart and all have a hand in the government of the house — her worry and vexation turning over and over, swallowing insult and choking back her voice, can scarcely be spoken of. And in a house of poverty and ruin, with no cooking-fire morning or night, she lives by her needle; there are things that cannot be told in full. How could she look to me for a lifetime, and I cast her off midway? What then of reason and feeling? This is the poem of the eastern expedition in the Juan Er — its tender feeling and gentle music, drawn out and portrayed, is the first righteousness of kingly transformation. And to delight in wife and children, to make the household peaceful, to obey father and mother — truly these are auspicious and good deeds.

Gu Kai treated his wife with propriety. Every night he entered and every morning he went out, and she seldom saw his face. When his illness grew grave, his wife came out to visit him. Kai had his attendants raise him up and put on his cap and added robes, and when he had finished expressing his care and encouragement, he at once told his wife to return. From this we see that between husband and wife, how can there be a single moment without propriety, so as to bring about the fault of excessive familiarity? Yet what else is propriety? To be harmonious and yet to have measure, to love and yet to respect each other — that is all.

Wang Balang of Luocheng was fierce by nature and loved to beat his wife. He doted on a courtesan, and the family property was all squandered. His wife being pressed by hunger and cold, he beat her the more urgently. At her wits' end, the wife asked kinsmen and neighbors to settle it between them; Balang had his wife and children live apart while he shared a room with the courtesan. Before long he fell ill and his property was exhausted, and the courtesan drifted away and left him. He went back to his wife, and his wife avoided him. He died suddenly, and his wife died too. Kinsmen and neighbors laid their two bodies in one place. In the night the sound of quarreling and cursing was suddenly heard; they opened the door and looked, and the two corpses were standing back to back.

The husband is the heaven of the wife, the one she depends on all her life. How can she not respect him? She who does not respect him is either a shrew or a loose woman; she may meet him with evil words, or curse him and work spells upon him. She does not know that to be born in a woman's body is for the most part a former condemnation; if she further wrongs her husband, she falls into the evil paths the deeper. And when the husband dies, before the flesh and bones are cold she thinks of marrying again, and looks on the sons and daughters she bore as strangers on the road. If she cannot mourn him in death, can she respect him in life?

Du Qi was a timid and weak man. His wife, Lady Zhang, always made light of him. In later years he grew sickly, and Zhang did not give him a single glance. Before long Zhang died before Qi did. After the burial the coffin burst open and she turned into a python and ran straight into the woods. Ah! The husband is the wife's heaven; to slight the husband is to slight heaven. Can heaven be slighted? Let each think on it.

In the Later Han, Liang Hong married a daughter of the Meng family named Guang. She first entered his house in finery, and for seven days Hong did not answer her. The wife then bound up her hair in a simple knot and put on plain cloth and worked as before. Hong was delighted and said: “This is truly Liang Hong's wife.” So they went together into hiding in the mountains of Baling. Later, to escape trouble, they went to Wu and lodged under the eaves of Gao Botong's house, hiring themselves out to pound grain for others. Whenever he came home, his wife would set out food for him and did not dare look up in his presence, raising the tray — that is, the bowl — level with her eyebrows. Botong said: “That hireling can make his wife respect him like this — he is no ordinary man.” So he gave them lodging in his house.

Du Gui was blind. His wife prayed day and night to the North Pole Star, and every bow was exactly seven times seven, forty-nine in number. In the end she was able to move the True Martial Lord to send down a transformation body and descend to heal him, and he could see as clearly as before.

Lady Li, wife of Yuwen Bangyan, worked hard to establish the household. She loved to read and understood the general sense of books, and with her own hand she copied and compiled passages to assist her husband; and she strictly supervised her sons in their studies. Her sons, led by Shuai, indeed passed the imperial examination and rose through the Hanlin and the Secretariat, reaching the office of Right Administration Commissioner, and their native place honored them. To this day there survives Lady Li's hand-copied collection of imperial edicts and proclamations.

Huang Guan of the Ming was a man of Anqing. In the Jianwen era he took the imperial examination as first in all three stages, and rose to be Grand Secretary. When the troops of the Jingnan campaign came, Guan died. His wife, Lady Weng, and both their daughters were taken. An order was issued that she be given to an elephant-keeper as wife. Weng made a pretext, saying that at the time of the troubles she had left a certain amount of gold in the keeping of close kin outside the city, and that if she and her children went to fetch it they would get it, but otherwise it would surely be hidden away. The elephant-keeper, greedy for the goods, went with them outside the city. The wife said: “The two girls must tie their skirts to mine for fear of losing each other in the crowd.” The slave agreed. The two girls did not understand their mother's purpose. When they came to the riverbank, she pulled the two girls and all three drowned together. To this day a temple is kept for them on the bank of the Qinhuai River.

Lady Zheng of Chongguo in the Song was the mother of Ouyang Xiu. Lord Chongguo passed the imperial examination and died while serving his second term as judge. Xiu was just four years old, and the family was poor. His mother labored with her own hands for food and clothing in order to support Xiu's study, and taught him his letters. Once on a snowy night she raked apart the cold ashes and wrote characters to teach him. In ordinary days she would weep and tell Xiu: “Your father was upright and loved to give. I did not live long enough to serve your grandparents, yet I know that your father could support his parents. I cannot know that you will succeed, yet I know that your father will have descendants. When I came to your father, it was more than a year since the mourning was ended; and at every sacrifice he would surely weep, and whenever he met with wine and meat he would surely weep, grieving that he could not support them. At first I thought it was only because he had newly put off mourning, and so for a time; but afterward it was always so, even to the end of his life, never otherwise. By this I know that your father could support his parents. Your father was an official, and once at night he was looking at the penal records and sighed again and again, saying: ‘I seek a way to let him live and cannot find it — that is what is pitiable.’ Turning his head, he saw your nurse holding you standing beside him, and he pointed at you and said: ‘My fate should be an early death; I fear I shall not live to see my son grown. You must tell him what I have said.’ In teaching his juniors he always followed this. By this I know that your father will have descendants.” Thereupon Xiu was moved to tears and strove at his studies until he passed the imperial examination and became noble and eminent, yet kept to frugality and plainness as before. Presently, for his frank remonstrance, he was demoted, and his lady said with a smile as always: “Poverty and lowliness are what we are used to. You must be at peace in it.” Xiu in the end became a worthy chancellor for his loyalty and uprightness, and his mother was many times enfeoffed as Grand Lady of Yue. Now of the ways of respecting a husband, which is greater than the two matters of fulfilling one's integrity and teaching one's sons? Therefore I place these two cases in order as the highest standard of respecting a husband. Let every wife take them to heart.

Laozi said: He who does not show himself is therefore illumined; he who does not justify himself is therefore of merit; he who does not boast of himself therefore endures. The Book of Changes says: The way of Heaven diminishes the full and benefits the modest; the way of Earth changes the full and flows toward the modest; the ghosts and gods harm the full and bless the modest. The modest is honored and shines; being lowly, it cannot be overstepped — this is the end of the gentleman. Great Yu did not boast and did not brag; foolish men and foolish women all said, “Each of us can surpass him” — yet he cut through the Dragon Gate, opened a passage at Yique, and made the earth level and Heaven complete, and his merit covered ten thousand generations. The Duke of Zhou was neither proud nor grudging; he labored in modesty and lowered himself to scholars; and in the eastern expedition he broke the ax and in the end brought peace to the house of Zhou. Therefore it is said: Truly great sages and great worthies all bring forth their work out of trembling and fear, as though standing on the brink of a deep gulf, as though treading on thin ice. Great Yu and the Duke of Zhou were sages — did they ever boast of their virtue to others? If so, then what do the men of today mean by their reckless boasting? It only shows that they do not know their own measure.

Gu Yong of the Han was enfeoffed as a marquis three days before his family knew of it. Xie An of the Jin played chess with a guest when the dispatch of victory arrived, and the guest never noticed anything. Cao Wuhui of the Song, having taken the south of the Yangtze, went in to have audience, and in the report sent up by the palace gate he wrote only that he had returned from the imperial commission to attend to public business in Jiangnan. Duke Wen Lu of the Song, in the Zhihe era, was the first to propose that Yingzong be made heir; and when Shenzong came to the throne, the duke spoke only of the merit of Han Qi, and the emperor thereby knew that he did not boast. All these gentlemen were of the very highest character and of the very greatest achievements, and still were modest and retiring and did not boast. Why do men not know to take them as their model?

He whose vessel is broad will surely have abundant blessing; he whose vessel is shallow will surely have thin blessing. Humility and fullness are the dividing line of calamity and fortune — how can one not be careful? And what is there in wealth, honor, and ability to rely upon? To be arrogant toward others with them, even apart from the calamity it brings, is first of all to lose one's heart and to know no shame.

Shi Chong of the Jin vied in wealth with Wang Kai. Kai made a purple silk screen for a march of forty li, and Chong made a brocade screen for fifty li to outdo him. Kai also once brought out a foot-long coral given him by the palace to boast before Chong, and Chong smashed it with an iron ruyi wand. Kai was furious, and Chong then brought out those he kept, all two or three feet long, and repaid him with one stalk. In other rare and precious things they contended for victory in every case. Later Chong was executed for a crime, and then he sighed, saying: “It is only that these slaves covet my wealth.” Ah! That single word of Chong's at the point of death — how clear it was! But had he known it earlier, he would surely not have boasted. Such was the cruelty of the calamity of boasting. Can the men of today be anything but careful in a single word or a single act?

Jealousy is found in both men and women. When a man sees another's rank and fame he is jealous; when he sees another's wealth and honor he is jealous; when another's position presses close to his own he resents it; when another's talent surpasses his own he resents it. All this is the working of a narrow and shallow capacity. As for women contending for favor and breeding resentment, they often bring ruin on the household and cut off its heirs, and their guilt is more than can be told. In life every man gnashes his teeth at them in hatred; in death they fall forever into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the realm of beasts — and even so it scarcely covers their guilt. That the man should set the standard by his own person — is that not his responsibility?

Pang Juan, a general of Wei in the Zhou, was jealous of Sun Bin's talent and had his feet cut off; afterward he was killed by Bin. In the Tang, Yu Chaoen and Cheng Yuanzhen were jealous of Guo Ziyi's merit and high position and rank, and schemed and slandered to harm him again and again; in the end they all incurred guilt — Yu Chaoen was executed and Cheng was exiled. In the Song, Han Tuozhou was jealous of Zhu Wengong Xi, then a compiler of the Huanzhang Pavilion, and so he formed a faction and denounced Xi as false learning, and for a time all the gentlemen were rejected and suppressed. Later Tuozhou was executed by Shi Miyuan. Shi Mingchen of the Northern Qi all his life deeply envied anyone who came out above him; afterward in the woods he turned into a python and went off toward the valley. It is recorded that Emperor Wu of Liang obtained a formula for stopping jealousy, and his attendants offered this saying: “May Your Majesty bestow it widely upon your ministers, so that the untalented may not envy the talented, the self-seeking may not envy the self-seeking, the muddy may not envy the clear, and the greedy may not envy the honest.” This too is one branch of urging men to goodness. The emperor agreed. If so, is jealousy only a matter for women?

Nü Zong was the wife of Su Bao of the Song in the Zhou. She served her mother-in-law with great filial piety. Su took office in Wei and after three years married a wife abroad. Her husband's elder brother's wife told her of it, and Nü Zong said: “A woman takes single-mindedness as her chastity and good compliance as her obedience. How could taking sole possession of her husband's love be her goodness? By the rites, a great officer may have three, and a knight two. My husband is a knight; that he has two, is it not fitting? Moreover, a wife may be put away for seven causes, and jealousy is the first of them. You do not tell me the rules of the household, but instead would have me commit an act that gets me cast off?” When the Duke of Song heard of it, he had her gate honored with a plaque and named her Nü Zong.

Lu Bian's uncle was magistrate of Hucheng, and Bian went to visit him. In a dream he came to a place where there were ten great millstones, and around the millstones were countless women. The millstones turned by themselves, and the ox-headed guards scooped up the women with great winnowing baskets and cast them into the hole of the mill, and they came out with the grinding, their bones and flesh crushed to powder, and the sound of their pain was hard to hear. Among the crowd Bian saw his uncle's wife, the wife of the magistrate of Hucheng. They met with grief and joy, and Bian asked for what cause these suffered such punishment. She said: “For jealousy.” Ah! So does hell requite jealousy. Dreadful, dreadful.

Liang Renyu favored a servant girl. His wife, Lady Li, was jealous and cruel: she bound the girl and beat her on the head. The girl cried out: “I am a servant of low birth, with no control over myself. Why must you lock my neck in irons and torment me so cruelly?” More than a month after the servant girl died, Lady Li fell ill, and the girl tormented her constantly. Four sores broke out on her head, and she wailed and screamed, and her skull rotted away and she died.

Guo, the wife of Jia Chong of the Jin, was jealous by nature. She once bore a son, and the wet nurse held him, and Chong went to him and stroked him. Guo had the wet nurse whipped to death. The child missed his nurse and wept himself to death. In the end Chong had no heir. Jia Chong was a great villain who ruined the state, and so a jealous wife cut off his line — this is the way of Heaven. Yet in the world those whose lines are cut off through jealousy are indeed not few. Let such a jealous wife give no thought to the depth of her sin and the greatness of her evil, and to the retribution of hell she cannot escape; but does she never think of the desolate grave of her line cut off before her eyes, the bones scattered, wind and rain grieving over the soul in the dark terrace, cattle and sheep trampling the pasture, and at the Cold Food Festival and Qingming, who will pour out a cup of water? Wild mist and rank grass, and ghosts weeping in the chill — for what cause is this? How sad! When my words come to this, I cannot but grieve and ache on behalf of such people, and cry aloud and sigh long. Let every wife think of it while there is yet time. Yet let me look again at the case of Jia Chong: that his line was cut off was the way of Heaven; and that a jealous wife came forth from his house was also a cunning turn of evil retribution. How can the husband then fail to think of piling up virtue to turn back Heaven, and instead only blame the jealousy of the woman?

In the Later Wei, the wife of Du Chang was Lady Liu. She was exceedingly jealous. There was a servant girl named Jinjing; when Chang bathed, he had her comb his hair, and Liu cut off both her fingers. Before long Liu was stung by a fox's spine, and both her fingers fell off. There was another servant girl named Yulian who could sing, and Chang loved her, and Liu cut out her tongue. Later Liu's own tongue rotted with sores, and when the matter became urgent she went to Chan Master Chou to repent. The master said: “You, madam, cut off a servant girl's fingers, and your own fingers have fallen; you cut out a servant girl's tongue, and your own tongue is severed. If you repent with a sincere heart, then you may escape.” Lady Liu bowed in worship and begged for mercy. After seven days the Chan master had her open her mouth wide and recited a spell over her. Two snakes came out of her mouth, more than a foot long; he recited the spell urgently, and they fell to the ground, and her tongue was restored. And from then on she was no longer jealous. Now when a man repents and mends his evil, gods and men alike are glad. However boundless the karma of sin you have made, only repent from now on and do not repeat it, and the former guilt melts like ice in a moment. This case is clear proof. To take warning from it and repent is truly a great blessing.
