Alas! The resentful wife has no good end, for a woman's feelings are easily knotted. Therefore cruel, venomous, and treacherous deeds she does in her own person without hesitation. It rests with the parents and brothers of the woman's own house: if she is not yet married, to guide her beforehand; if she is married, to restrain her with tact and not to feed her flame. Then perhaps the heart of jealousy may be somewhat stilled. And to mediate and transform her from within is the husband's part. As for him who pursues women and gives rein to lust, so that the lion of the eastern river roars, the gentleman will hold that the guilt of the lewd husband is by far the lighter.

Treat a wife with harmony and respect; treat a son with strictness and uprightness. To treat a wife without propriety is to lose the meaning of husband and wife as one answering the other; to teach a son without the Way is to wound the grace of engendering and rearing him. To be unrighteous and unkind is altogether to be without conduct. Those who treat their wives today: if not harsh and stingy with affection, then overfamiliar without measure. Those who treat their sons: if not too indulgent, then certainly too severe. When one has no conduct oneself, how can one reprove wife and son?

Zhang Zhan of the Later Han was grave and strict and loved propriety; in his daily conduct he was always respectful. Whenever he met with his wife and sons he would set forth the instructions of propriety and good words and excellent deeds to teach them, like a stern lord governing his ministers. Therefore his wife also admonished him and improved herself in turn, and their good name was heard in the district. This case may serve well as a model for teaching wife and sons.

Shi Tang married while still of low estate. When he passed the imperial examination, he resented that he had not got a daughter of a rich house for a wife, and repented of it. So day by day he kept apart from her and no longer slept in the same bed. His wife's heart grew heavy and she fell ill. For several years Tang did not give her a single glance, and his wife too swallowed her resentment. As she was dying she called to Tang through the wall, saying: “I am dying now. Can you bear not to look at me once?” Tang never turned to look. A year after his wife's death, the courts of the underworld condemned him for his wicked and heartless conduct and cut away his years and emoluments, and he died of a sudden illness.

Wang Yao of Zhuozhou doted on his two sons and fostered vicious natures in them; unable to control them, he reported them to the officials. Both sons died, and his line was cut off. When Yao died, on the night of the fifteenth day of the second month of the following year, Liu Jin, a temple attendant at the local City God's temple, saw a man holding a petition and begging for offerings at Qingming. The City God said angrily: “You had sons and could not teach them, and you cut off your own line yourself. Who can make offerings to you?” He ordered the ghost guards to drive him out. The man went off weeping aloud. The temple keeper inquired after him the next day, and learned that Yao had been dead more than a year. The old saying goes: The sons of Confucius' house did not know how to curse; the sons of Zengzi's house did not know how to quarrel — habit had made their nature. It says also: Raise sons and younger brothers as you raise the orchid and the angelica: you pile up learning to cultivate them and pile up goodness to moisten them. Between father and son one must not dote with a small tenderness; from youth restrain them with strictness and bind them with law, and then when grown they will not bring the regret of unworthiness. It says also: When a man has several sons, the love shown in food and clothing must not be unequal; the distinction of elder and younger, honored and humble, must not be slack; the difference between worthy and unworthy, right and wrong, must not be undiscerned. Show them equality when young, and when grown they will have no trouble of contending over wealth; reprove them with strictness when young, and when grown they will have no trouble of insolence and contempt; teach them to distinguish when young, and when grown they will have no trouble of joining evil company. Looking over all these sayings together, a man may know what to take as his model.

A wife should serve her husband's father and mother exactly as a son serves his own father and mother: with a lowly spirit and a cheerful countenance and a soft voice, sharing their warmth and cold in her own body, feeling their sickness and pain and itch and ache as her own concern, supporting them in going out and coming in. If she fails in propriety even a little, that is unfilial, and the guilt of it reaches to Heaven, and thunder and fire will strike at once. Ah! But I have something further to say. A wife is joined to her husband's parents by man; a son is joined to his parents by Heaven. From ancient times, a son who is unfilial to his parents while the wife alone is filial to her husband's parents — I fear there is no such principle. Therefore every failure of propriety in a wife is brought about by her husband. Would the gods' punishment and the ghosts' censure fall upon the woman alone? Let every son take this to heart.

On the twenty-second day of the third month of the fifth year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming, in Shanyang County of Huai'an, Feng, the wife of Mao Jizong, was filial by nature to the utmost. Her mother-in-law was old and gravely ill, and Mao was away transporting grain to the capital. The wife bathed and changed her clothes, and at night cried out to Heaven to die in her mother-in-law's place. She took a knife and cut into her own side, and the tip of her liver sprang out. Suddenly she heard her child cry; fearing it would wake her mother-in-law, she covered the wound with a kerchief and went in to soothe the child. Then, thinking that so small a piece of liver would not be enough to heal her, she prayed devoutly and cut again. The moon had not yet risen, when the sky suddenly became bright and clear and the stars all shone, lighting the wife's body as bright as day. She cut a leaf of liver from her belly and at once made it into broth and brought it to her mother-in-law. As soon as the old woman tasted it she felt it wondrously sweet, and asked what it was. The wife made the excuse that a neighbor had got a deer: it was deer's liver. The old woman ate it all, and her illness healed at once. So it was that her utmost sincerity moved Heaven, and the wound did not pain her; but the traces of blood could not be hidden. Her husband's younger sister noticed it, and the whole household was astonished and told of it. Only then did her mother-in-law know that she had saved her. She wept bitterly and was moved and pitied her. For a time the scholars and gentlemen of the district joined in a petition to the throne, but through the exactions of the petty clerks it could not reach the emperor. Happily there was Jiang Tianyi, a licentiate of Huizhou, who wrote A Collection of Wondrous Filial Piety Shaking Heaven to make the matter known.

Jia Dan of the Song was military commissioner of Huazhou. At that time there was a woman of the people who served her mother-in-law unfilial. The mother-in-law was old and blind, and the woman served her foul food. The old woman wondered at its taste, and when her son came home from outside he took it and questioned his wife. When the son saw it he wept aloud toward Heaven, and suddenly thunder crashed and a swift stroke cut off the woman's head and joined a dog's head to her body. Dan learned of it and had her led about within the borders of the province as a warning to the unfilial. Alas, alas! Men today are quick to say that a woman is of watery nature and cannot be established in teaching. How far this saying is from reason! Nowadays, in the days when she is a girl, her parents have already failed in the method of teaching and rearing; and when she is a wife, her foolish husband lacks the benefit of a model to observe. Thus the evils of disobedience, lewdness, and jealousy come to seem impossible to restrain. But if those who are her parents, from childhood to the binding of her hair, would open her heart with filial piety, respect, gentleness, and compliance, then even though she marry a man without talent, she could still know how to establish herself; how much more when the one who sets her the pattern is a filial, brotherly, good, and kind gentleman! The teaching of daughters and the teaching of sons are of equal weight — this saying should truly be made known to all the world.

The ancestral spirits are the spirits of one's forebears. Whenever the dressing of the dead and the encoffining are without propriety, the mourning without rule, the burial not made in due time, the fasting and sacrifice not sincere, the sweeping of the graves not diligent, the ancestral hall not kept in order, and the incense and lamp broken and intermittent — all these are slights. Now the water has its source and the tree its root: how dare one forget them even for a moment? If one fails in this, I do not know what can be said for him.

Crown Prince Zhaoming of Liang was of the utmost goodness and filial piety. When Lady Ding the Consort, who bore him, died, he would not let water or gruel pass his lips, and at every bout of weeping he fainted away. Emperor Wu instructed him, saying: “Grief must not destroy the nature. I am here — how can you carry on so?” Only then did the crown prince force himself to take a few mouthfuls; and from that time to the burial he took a pint of wheat gruel a day. The crown prince's body had always been stout, and his belt measured ten spans; by this time he had wasted away by more than half. Whenever he went in to court, officials and common folk who saw him could not but weep.

Chen Gao came to the capital as a tribute student and prayed for a dream at a temple of the gods. In the dream a god said to him: “Your father's coffin is not yet buried. Rank and fame are not to be asked about yet.” Chen did not believe it. The next year he was failed at the examination hall, and so he went home and hurried to complete the burial. When he took the examination again, he passed at last. The Ledger of Merits and Demerits says: He who does not bury his parents within three years of their death, for each month of delay incurs ten demerits. He who buries them without doing his utmost, or lets the grave be damaged, incurs a hundred demerits. He who does not mend it at once after becoming aware, for each day of delay incurs ten demerits. It says also: To sacrifice to one's forebears at the wrong season and without reverence incurs one demerit; and if it is because of pleasure-seeking that the season is missed, that is five times more.

Whenever Deng Zuoming swept the graves, he would linger in the graveyard and return only after a whole day, saying: “In the space of a year, how many days do I come here? I cannot bear to go away as if it did not matter.” Words of the utmost goodness! Nowadays, by the custom of the world, once at the year's festivals and at Qingming one visits the graves, and the rest of the time one leaves one's parents in the wild waste and gives them no thought. At the sacrifice one mostly joins with brothers, kinsmen, and friends in giving free rein to pleasure and roaming, and returns having enjoyed it to the full. The year's festival is no sweeping of the pines; it is only admiring the plum blossom. Qingming is no visiting of the graves; it is only treading the green. Alas! If emolument does not reach one's parents, what good is it to fill wife and children? If in life one stinted them of coarse food and water, what use is it to set out the full array of tripods after death?

A minister receives his charge from his lord; a son from his parent; a disciple from his teacher. All who stand below and receive their charge from those above — it is the charge of a superior. If what is commanded cannot rightly be done, one should still bend every effort to move him and remonstrate beforehand; then one has not dared to accept the charge. If what is commanded may rightly be done, then to carry it out without effort is still a fault — how much more to defy it? Defiance is where rebellious ministers and traitorous sons come from.

Tao An of the Ming was a man of Dangtu. Taizu appointed An magistrate of Huangzhou, instructing him: “Cherish well the common folk.” An reverenced the imperial charge. When he came to the prefecture he remitted taxes and corvée, lightened heavy labor, diligently instructed the scholars, and reduced punishments and penalties, and the people all rejoiced and submitted. He was recalled to be a Hanlin scholar and promoted to the Jiangxi provincial administration as assistant administrator. In whatever had no cause for evasion he gave his whole heart and strength to match the imperial charge. When An died, the emperor himself composed a text to sacrifice to him, granted him a posthumous title, and extended the privilege to his sons; his sons and grandsons all passed the imperial examination and rose to the offices of ministers and assistants. Now those today who are to cherish and govern the black-haired people all look up to and receive the charge of their ruler. Yet they are cruel and tyrannical toward living beings and do injury to the common folk, giving not the least thought to our ruler's heart of teaching and rearing — what guilt of defiance could exceed this? The common folk can indeed do nothing about it. But do they know that Heaven's mirror is not far, that the people may not be tyrannized over, and Heaven may not be cheated?

All things in the world turn to emptiness in a moment. Only the piling up of virtue and the doing of good, the promoting of benefit and the removing of harm, and matters of that kind — world after world and life after life — go with one and are enjoyed, without end. Other things, such as mansions and terraces and ponds, clothes and food and carriages and horses, and all the affairs of poetry, painting, and rare curiosities, are all enough to lose one's purpose and burden the body. What good are they? As for hanging lanterns and putting on plays, singing songs and drinking wine, and games of chance and chess and the like, not only are they of no benefit — they are among the greatest harms. Shun them, shun them.

Zhang Yong of the Song, when he governed Chengdu, feared that the people would find food hard to come by and turn to banditry. He had the land tax of the various districts commuted to six hundred thousand hu of rice each year; and when spring came he would register the common folk, allotting each by the number of mouths a certificate to buy rice at the original price. By this means, even in years of famine and poor harvest, there was no great hunger. Chen Yaozuo was grain transport commissioner of Guangnan. It was the custom there not to take medicine: when ill, the people prayed to ghosts, and many died. The commissioner gathered tested prescriptions from his own household and had them carved in stone at the post stations, and the local people relied on them. Wang Di was magistrate of Chengdu. Many of the people practiced cremation, and the commissioner strictly forbade it, setting aside official land for public graveyards to bury the unburied, and from that the region had no more cremation. Su Shi was magistrate of Hangzhou. He dredged the two rivers, repaired the six wells, and built a long embankment planted with willows to secure the embankment's benefit, and the people named it the Su Embankment. Yu Zhongkuan was magistrate of Shunchang. The custom there was much drowning of infant girls. The commissioner wrote an exhortation and warning, summoned the elders to the veranda, earnestly comforted and encouraged them, and brought out the text to urge them, and the custom was wholly changed. All those above did what was beneficial. From this we know that a gentleman in the world values what benefits men and things; how could he merely talk grandly and argue broadly without practical result? As for us in cultivating our persons and rectifying ourselves and examining our past faults, there is truly more work than the days can hold; yet men recklessly undertake all kinds of useless doings, not knowing that this phantom body and phantom world in a flash return to extinction, and that only the one perfectly bright nature endures through ten thousand kalpas, never born and never dying. Why do men today, rather than idly whiling away the hours, dragging through water and mud, not do a little work within this?

A minister who cheats his lord, a son who defies his parent, a wife who turns her back on her husband, brothers who plunder each other, friends who undermine each other — all are the working of an outer heart. And it need not take shape in deed: as soon as a subtle stirring arises, men may not know it, but the ghosts and gods have already condemned the heart.

Qin Hui of the Song schemed in secret with the men of Jin and strove to uphold a peace settlement. Whenever our generals won a slight victory, he at once pressed them to withdraw their armies, and the cities and towns we gained were lost again immediately. He also had Yue Fei killed in prison. Later there was one who went to the underworld and saw Hui in the uninterrupted hell. Today, before the tomb of the Prince of Yue in Hangzhou, iron statues of Hui and his wife kneel; visitors beat them and urine on them to vent their hatred.

A certain man of Yuezhong in the Ming treated his wife with deep affection. But the wife came to long for a youth of the neighborhood, and the two would look at each other from time to time. Though she dwelt in the same room with her husband, her heart thought only of the youth. Later her husband fell ill and died, and before the mourning was ended she married the youth. That night she dreamed that her former husband came and said: “That you married after my death I do not reproach. But that while I lived you cherished an outer heart — that is truly hateful.” Thereupon he took an iron mallet and struck her on the back, and soon after she vomited blood and died.

This sentence speaks of cursing when there is no right to seek vindication: whenever in anger a man curses himself and also curses others. This is the first omen of disaster called down by the petty man and the woman, and often before death comes, what they have cursed comes to pass at once. How can one not take warning?

The wife of Yan Dian had once been intimate with another man and had also stolen a handkerchief from a neighbor's house. The neighbor cursed and reviled her, and Dian then cursed himself and cursed the other, saying: “If my wife has indeed been intimate with a man and stolen your handkerchief, may I be struck by lightning; and if not, then you must take it.” Before long Dian was struck dead by the thunderbolt's axe, and beneath his ribs were written the words: “The fool protects his wife.” His wife too was struck dead, and beneath her ribs were written the words: “She practiced lewdness and stole.”

Zihan of the state of Zheng in the Zhou said: To have oaths and curses is the root of disorder. Now life and death have their fixed decree: it is not what one loves that can give life, nor what one hates that can kill. Yet men today curse themselves and curse others — how deluded, how foolish!

Partial hatred and partial love have a very wide reach. In every case — the lord toward his minister, the father toward his son, the husband toward wife and concubine, the master toward his servants — it is found. But among women it is worst between those before and after her and between wife and concubine. Therefore Zengzi, when his wife died, did not marry again for the rest of his life, saying: “Emperor Gaozong, because of a second wife, brought about the death of Xiaoji; Yin Jifu, because of a second wife, brought about the death of Boqi. I am not the equal of Gaozong above, nor the match of Jifu in the middle; how could I be free of the same fault?” Excellent! This is one who feared to have partial hatred and partial love, and so preserved a father's grace whole. Yet not to marry again after a wife's death is what human feeling finds hard. Let one only seek, after marrying again, always to realize Zengzi's words; then perhaps one will not go greatly astray.

Xu Jia of the Eastern Sea had by his former wife, Lady Xu, a son named Tiejie. When Xu died, he married again, a Lady Chen, who was fierce and jealous and wished to kill the son of the former wife. Chen bore a son, and named him Tiechu — the iron pestle — meaning to pound the mortar, Tiejie. Tiejie was given over to every kind of beating, and died of cold and hunger at the age of sixteen. More than ten days after his death, his ghost suddenly came home and said: “I am Tiejie. My mother has appealed her grievance to Heaven and obtained a warrant from the celestial court to come and wipe out the wrong. Let Tiechu die of sickness, and let him suffer as I suffered.” Chen tried a hundred schemes to avert it, and could not. At that time Tiechu was six years old. Suddenly his belly swelled and his body ached, and his whole body turned black and purple, and he died.

In the Zhou of the Northern Wei there was a compassionate mother, a daughter of the Mengyang family, who was the second wife of Mang Mao. She bore three sons, and her husband's former wife had left five sons, none of whom loved the mother; yet the mother treated them most generously, and still the five sons did not love her. The compassionate mother then had it that her own three sons should not be ranked with the former wife's sons: in clothing and food, in rising and resting, in advancing and withdrawing, they were kept far apart. Still the five sons of the former wife did not love her. Before long the middle son of the former wife broke the command of the King of Wei and was condemned to death. The compassionate mother grieved and lamented, and toiled morning and evening to save him. Someone said: “The son does not love the mother, and that to the utmost. Why do you labor and fear for him like this?” The compassionate mother said: “My own sons, even if they do not love me, I must still save them from calamity and rid them of guilt. Now toward the former wife's son it is otherwise: how would that differ from having no mother at all? His father, because the boy was orphaned, made me his stepmother. A stepmother is a mother to him; if she does not love her son, can she be called compassionate? To be fond of one's own and neglect those who came before — can that be called righteous? Uncompassionate and unrighteous, how could I stand in the world? Though he does not love me, can I recklessly forsake righteousness?” So she persuaded the King of Wei, who admired her righteousness and pardoned the son and restored his household. From that time the five sons drew close to the compassionate mother in affection, harmonious as though of one mother. And she trained and guided the eight sons by propriety and righteousness, and all of them became great officers and ministers of Wei.

To overstep is to stride across. A well benefits and succors very widely; it has a spring god presiding over it, named Guan, whose form is like a beautiful woman. And the water in a well both profits the multitude of living beings and is used besides to sacrifice to the gods and make offerings to the Buddhas — how can it be profaned? The stove is one of the five sacrifices; it is the Great One, the Fire God, surnamed Zhang, named Zhuo, styled Ziguo. He governs the lives of high and low in a single household; he specially observes the length and shortness of good and evil, and foreknows good and ill fortune. To overstep it is to profane and insult the divine spirits, and the guilt of it is very great. And this is not only striding over it: to sit on the well-curb, to tread on the stove door, to dry foul things over it, and the like, are all defilements and profanations.

Zhang Xiaoxian, when drunk with wine, loved to jump into wells for sport. One day a golden-armored god in the well thrust at him with a spear, and Xiaoxian's belly pained him greatly, constantly as though pierced by a lance. Only after devout prayer did he heal.
